question: According to the most recent report by the IPCC1, the Mediterranean is one of the most vulnerable climate hotspots in the world, where there is a 99% probability that extreme weather phenomena will increase more than the global average.

Despite this, in the draft law2 that was submitted for expedited consultation, the Greek Government is abolishing the minimum undeveloped zone extending 30 metres from the shoreline, permitting its full ‘commercial’ development, while other Member States are putting in place legal protection for undeveloped coastal zones that are at least 100 metres wide and may extend as far as 250 metres from the shoreline.

Is this draft law consistent with Article 8 of the Protocol on Integrated Coastal Zone Management in the Mediterranean (2009/89/ΕC), which the EU has ratified and which is binding on all Member States, and under which coastal zones may not be less than 100 metres in width? Should the whole of the European coastline be subject to the same adaptation standards?

Is this draft law consistent with the EU biodiversity strategy for 2030 and the EU strategy on adaptation to climate change, under which coastal areas must be protected in terms of the restoration of ecosystems and the protection of human life?

answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (22.4.2024) 1. The Barcelona Convention Protocol on Integrated Coastal Zone Management in the Mediterranean (ICZM Protocol)1 provides a legal framework for the integrated management of coastal zones. The Protocol requires that national legal frameworks allow for the protection and sustainable use of the coastal zone, which may not be less than 100 metres.

By ratifying the ICZM Protocol, countries commit to turning their legally binding provisions into national law and to ensuring compliance and enforcement. Despite the strong encouragement of the Commission, Greece has not yet ratified the ICZM Protocol. 2.

While the EU Biodiversity Strategy2 and the EU Strategy on Adaptation to Climate Change3 express concern about the effects of climate change on coastal areas and consider that the protection and restoration of coastal ecosystems could strengthen coastal defence and climate resilience, those strategies do not contain specific legally binding obligations for Member States.

The European Climate Law4 requires Member States to ensure progress in climate adaptation and promote nature-based solutions and ecosystem-based adaptation. In its assessment of the progress on climate adaptation5, the Commission indicated that Greece should include in the relevant strategies coastal floods and found that those strategies have not focused enough on nature-based solutions.

The Commission recommended that Greece assess vulnerabilities and risks related to floods, prepare a comprehensive assessment and take action to ‘promote nature-based solutions and ecosystem-based adaptation in national strategies, policies and plans and provide investments for their deployment’6.
